lines.text: Platinum was once thrown into rivers.
In colonial Colombia, miners kept finding heavy silvery grit in their gold.

scene.label: Placer platinum grains
scene.credit: Photo: James St. John, CC BY 2.0

lines.text: They called it platina, meaning little silver.
lines.say: They called it plah tee nuh, meaning little silver.

lines.text: The tools of the day could not melt it.
But its weight and shine let it pass as gold.

scene.label: A platinum nugget, replica
scene.credit: Photo: James St. John, CC BY 2.0

lines.text: Officials banned mining in rich platina deposits until 1726.
lines.say: Officials banned mining in rich plah tee nuh deposits until seventeen twenty six.

lines.text: Mines reopened only if they threw the platina back into rivers.
lines.say: Mines reopened only if they threw the plah tee nuh back into rivers.

lines.text: In 1731, sacks of raw platinum were dumped into the Bogota River.
lines.say: In seventeen thirty one, sacks of raw platinum were dumped into the Boh goh tah River.

lines.text: One dumping spot was named the Platina Gorge.
lines.say: One dumping spot was named the Plah tee nuh Gorge.

lines.text: In 1787, a royal order made platina the Crown's property.
lines.say: In seventeen eighty seven, a royal order made plah tee nuh the Crown's property.

post.caption: Platinum was once thrown into rivers. In colonial Colombia, miners kept finding heavy silvery grit in their gold. They called it platina, meaning little silver. The tools of the day could not melt it. But its weight and shine let it pass as gold. Officials banned mining in rich platina deposits until 1726. Mines reopened only if they threw the platina back into rivers. In 1731, sacks of raw platinum were dumped into the Bogota River. One dumping spot was named the Platina Gorge. In 1787, a royal order made platina the Crown's property. Photo: James St. John, CC BY 2.0.
